title: Smallest Sparrow in the Hedge
part: PART ONE: LIGHT WIND FROM THE WEST

pages.text:
*Sky Report: light wind from the west, clear, one very small bird with very big ideas.*

Pip was the smallest sparrow in Thistlewick Hedge, which is a thing you could have worked out for yourself by looking at her, or by listening to the other sparrows, who mentioned it often.

"Smallest sparrow in the hedge," said Uncle Dorn, as he did every morning, "and smallest she'll stay."

Pip was eleven weeks old and weighed less than a walnut. She stood on the topmost twig with her toes curled tight and her chest puffed out, and she looked at the sky, which was very large, and she thought: *Yes. That one. I'll have that one.*

The wind lifted the tip of her crooked left tail feather and set it down again, the way you might tap a friend on the shoulder. Pip decided it was a yes.
pages.image: A tiny round brown-streaked sparrow with a crooked left tail feather stands puffed-up on the topmost twig of a hedge at sunrise, looking at a huge pink-gold sky; a plump gloomy older sparrow watches from a branch below.

pages.text:
Mornings in Thistlewick Hedge were loud. Two hundred sparrows woke at once and began to argue about seeds, weather, and who had taken whose branch. Mother Wren, who had opinions on everything, gave them all out before breakfast. Somebody's aunt announced that there was a worm in the east corner. Somebody's uncle announced that the worm was hers.

The fledglings measured everything in wingbeats. How far to the fence post: forty wingbeats. How far to the pond: ninety. How far you could fly before landing was the only thing anyone your age ever really wanted to know.

At the top of the hedge, Cinder, the biggest fledgling of the year, did a slow loop as smooth as a ribbon, and the whole hedge applauded. Pip took a running hop off her twig and tried the same. What came out was a wobble, a spin, and a splash landing in the pond. There was a pause. Then two hundred sparrows laughed, not cruelly, but the way you laugh at a hat that has blown off.

Pip climbed out. She shook herself. Her crooked tail feather dripped.
pages.image: A tiny sparrow climbs dripping out of a puddle at the base of a hedge while a crowd of laughing sparrows watches; high above, a large glossy chestnut sparrow does an elegant loop in the sky.

pages.text:
Here is how Pip came to be so small. She hatched a full week after her brothers and sisters, the runt of the clutch, and fell out of the nest before she could fly, which is how she got the crooked feather. Two autumns ago her parents flew into a storm over the sea, and did not come back.

After that there was only Uncle Dorn, who was plump and gloomy and roughly the shape of a cushion. He had taken her in with a great deal of grumbling, and had grumbled ever since, every day, with more love than he knew how to say and a great deal more worry than he knew what to do with.

"Small birds stay low," he told her each night, as he tucked her under his wing. "Low is safe. Low is warm. Low never got blown out to sea."

Pip, half asleep against his soft grey feathers, did not argue. She had stopped arguing months ago. She had started something else instead. It was a plan, and it was still too small and tender to say out loud.
pages.image: A plump gloomy grey-brown sparrow tucks a tiny sparrow with a crooked tail feather under his wing at night on a branch under a starry sky.

pages.text:
Nettle found her at the seed patch. Nettle was Pip's best friend: a skinny, freckled, anxious sparrow with feet too large for the rest of her, who watched clouds the way other birds watched the ground.

"They're announcing it at sundown," Nettle whispered. Her eyes were huge. "The Trial of Three Winds."

Pip dropped her seed.

Every bird in the hedge knew about the Trial. Once a year, at the Gathering, the Elders chose the flock's new Storm-Sparrows: the fastest, boldest scouts, the ones who rode the edge of the autumn gales far ahead of the flock and read the sky for the safe way south across the Grey Sea. It was the only thing in the world Pip had ever really wanted. And it had never, in the whole history of Thistlewick Hedge, been given to a bird who weighed less than a walnut.

Her heart turned over like a leaf in a gust.
pages.image: Two young sparrows, one tiny with a crooked tail and one skinny and freckled with big feet, whisper together over a scatter of seeds in a sunny meadow of tall grass; the tiny one has dropped a seed.

pages.text:
At sundown the whole flock crowded onto the Gathering Rock, wing to wing, and Elder Marra rose above them.

Marra was big, and grey, and streaked like an old stone wall, with a torn wing tip and a voice like a cart on a gravel road. She told them the Trial would be flown at sunrise, three days from now, over the three winds of the coast. Any fledgling might enter, she said, "except those the Elders judge unready."

Her eye moved over the crowd. It passed over Pip. It stopped, for the smallest possible instant, and moved on.

That was all. Nobody else noticed. But Pip felt it land on her like a raindrop, and she sat very still, small and brown among the taller birds, with the pink light going gold on the rock.

"I'm entering," she said to the evening wind, so quietly that only the wind could have heard.

And the wind, for a wonder, lifted one feather in reply.
pages.image: A crowd of sparrows on a big sunset-lit rock listens to a large grey-streaked elder sparrow with a torn wing tip on a high ledge; in the crowd a tiny sparrow with a crooked tail looks up determinedly as a breeze ruffles her feather.
